text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive the dispersion relation from local tension and Coriolis forces, find the unstable band and maximum growth, and distinguish linear growth from transport saturation. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Connect a faster inner orbit to a slower outer orbit A Keplerian disk has angular velocity decreasing outward, but specific angular momentum j = r²Ω increasing outward. Even when hydrodynamic axisymmetric radial exchanges are stable, magnetic coupling changes the problem. This is the starting point of magnetorotational instability, MRI. q ≡ −d lnΩd ln r, κ² = 4Ω²+dΩ²d ln r = 2(2−q)Ω² Keplerian rotation has q = 3/2. The epicyclic frequency κ describes the oscillation of a slightly radially displaced orbit. Restrict the model to 0 ≤ q < 2, separating MRI from hydrodynamic Rayleigh instability. 02Magnetic tension acts like a weak spring Imagine two fluid elements connected by a field line. The faster inner element stretches the connection, so tension slows the inner element and accelerates the outer one. Losing angular momentum lets the inner element move inward, while the outer element moves outward. The separation can reinforce itself. Quantify this using a local rotating frame, ideal MHD, incompressibility, a uniform vertical field B, and axisymmetric disturbances with vertical wavenumber k. Define the Alfvén speed and a tension frequency squared K. vA = B√(μ₀ρ), K = k²vA² These are SI expressions. K is not a spring constant in force per length; it is a restoring coefficient per unit mass with units s−2. Even a weak field can provide appreciable tension at a sufficiently large wavenumber. 03Coupled displacement equations Let ξx be radial displacement and ξy azimuthal displacement. The linear local equations contain Coriolis forces, the differential-rotation tidal term, and tension. Take these equations as the ideal-MHD input, then derive their eigenvalues explicitly. ξ̈x−2Ωξ̇y = (2qΩ²−K)ξx ξ̈y+2Ωξ̇x = −Kξy Substitute ξ ∝ exp(st), replacing first and second derivatives by s and s². A nonzero displacement requires the determinant of the coefficient matrix to vanish. (s²+K−2qΩ²)ξx−2Ωsξy = 0 2Ωsξx+(s²+K)ξy = 0 s⁴+(κ²+2K)s²+K(K−2qΩ²) = 0 04Solve a quadratic in s squared Set b = kvA/Ω, z = s²/Ω², and κ̂² = 2(2−q). The quartic in s is a quadratic in z. A positive larger root permits an exponentially growing solution with s > 0. z²+(κ̂²+2b²)z+b²(b²−2q) = 0 z+ = −(κ̂²+2b²)+√(κ̂⁴+16b²)2 For 0 < q < 2, the interval 0 < b² < 2q makes the constant term negative, producing one positive and one negative root. There is no growth at exactly b = 0; sufficiently strong tension, b² ≥ 2q, also suppresses this mode. 05Find the fastest-growing wavelength Differentiate z+ with respect to b² and set the derivative to zero: −1 + 4/√(κ̂⁴+16b²) = 0. Rearrangement gives the optimum tension and maximum growth rate. bmax² = q(4−q)4, smax = qΩ2 q = 32 : bmax² = 1516, smax = 3Ω4 For Keplerian rotation the e-folding time is 4/(3Ω), about 0.21 of an orbit 2π/Ω. This is the linear growth time of a small perturbation, not a prediction of unlimited exponential amplification. 06MRI growth does not fix a saturated alpha A real mode must fit within the disk thickness. Resistivity, ambipolar diffusion, and other nonideal effects alter the result when field–gas coupling is weak. The ideal unstable band alone cannot establish activity throughout a protoplanetary disk. Linear eigenvalues do not determine nonlinear saturation or the mean transport stress. Obtaining the alpha used in an alpha disk requires additional calculations including field geometry, nonlinear interactions, and boundary conditions. Compare the clock for magnetic flux to slip relative to weakly ionized gas in ambipolar diffusion. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Fix the fastest-growing Keplerian mode. At fixed density and wavenumber, double the magnetic field. Does that mode still grow? Have all disk modes become stable? Show the answer and reasoning Its b² rises from 15/16 to 15/4, outside b² < 3, so that mode stops growing. Other, longer wavelengths can have smaller b; this is not stability of every mode. The wavelength must also fit within the real disk. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
